extracted.intended_audience: students, instructors, and scholars of mass communication / media studies
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and evaluating the outside-of-organization forces that shape news and media content (economic, technological, institutional, community, and ideological influences) as described in a media-studies textbook chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market structure / competition between newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a newspaper operates in a monopoly or competitive market may affect its content: competitive publishers face split readers and advertisers' dollars while monopolies are 'the only (newspaper) game in town.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies are mixed: some (Weaver & Mullins 1975; McCombs 1987) find virtually no editorial differences between competing newspapers; Utt & Pasternack (1985) find no graphics difference for similarly sized papers but smaller papers may be more modern in design; Lacy (1988) suggests intercity competition can increase local news coverage for suburban papers. Note the assumption that competition produces diversity is not always supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television market competition and positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Television stations rarely operate in monopoly environments; stations must 'find their own part of the mass audience' and position newscasts to draw viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atwater (1984) argues broadcast editors create diversity by differentiating their station's newscasts; roughly half of local TV stories in Atwater's study were unique to one station. This suggests station competition can increase informational diversity in news (especially news programming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of cable expansion on content diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Expansion of cable and increase in channel numbers does not automatically increase diversity of content offered to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gitlin (1985) notes most cable channel programs are supplied by a few distribution companies using Hollywood conventions; much cable content is reruns. Thus channel proliferation can coexist with homogenized content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global competition and international news providers
rubrics_metrics.description: The emergence of global news services (e.g., CNN, CNNI, BBC World, Reuters, Sky News, Euronews) creates a global market for news and affects international news coverage and language offerings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CNN's ascendancy after major world events; alliances between BBC and ABC; Reuters' role as supplier and creation of Spanish-language service with BBC/Telemundo; networks planning multi-language services to match competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market characteristics: community size and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Community size and local economy influence what kinds of media operate there and the content they produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carroll (1989) and Lacy & Bernstein (1988): larger TV/newspaper markets produce more spontaneous and local news and are likelier to generate original content; smaller markets rely more on features, preplanned stories, wire copy, and grassroots/legal advertising, possibly due to smaller budgets and staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic conditions and newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Nationwide economic changes can alter media assessments of newsworthiness, increasing coverage of sectors tied to market conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erfle & McMillan (1989): network coverage of the oil industry increases with oil prices; Sparkes (1978): bilateral coverage related to trade and GNP. McCombs' 'Constancy Hypothesis'—media spending grows with the general economy, so shifts in media growth reflect broader economic constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community relations and 'boosterism'
rubrics_metrics.description: Local publishers and stations may act as 'community boosters,' promoting economic development and sometimes sacrificing detachment and objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: newspapers running stories to attract industry or running campaigns to save military bases; content placement and editorial choices (front page vs. buried) may reflect boosterism; some journalists resist, asserting roles to report rather than cheerlead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader-driven content and audience research
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers and stations may alter content based on marketing and audience research to 'position' for a target audience (the 'reader-driven newspaper').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gannett's News 2000 program: tools include coupons soliciting ideas, public forums, focus groups, and shopper surveys. Results include fewer jumps, shorter stories, more graphics, and 'news-you-can-use' — critics argue this limits treatment of complex stories and reduces reporter time in the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser influence and economic dependency
rubrics_metrics.description: Because audiences are sold to advertisers, advertisers often influence media content and can push for changes; advertisers can also use economic retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising funds most broadcasting and large portions of print media (notes cite percentages). Advertiser-created programming and integrated commercials (hard-to-skip spots) are examples of advertisers shaping content. Economic retaliation (boycotts) can lead to self-censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest-group influence and PR/pseudoevents
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest groups attempt to influence media content via organized efforts and press guidelines; public relations practitioners create pseudoevents to control coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success is mixed; groups that can retaliate economically have more effect. Pseudoevents are a tactic by PR to shape media attention and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government regulation and legal constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Government exerts control through laws (e.g., libel) and regulations that affect who can own broadcast media and what content is permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governmental influence varies by country and takes concrete regulatory/legal forms that shape media ownership and permitted content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional affiliations and corporate ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Interlocking directorates and affiliations between media corporations and other elite institutions can influence media ideology and autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dreier and Han document boards of major newspapers sharing members with banks, law firms, etc.; such 'webs of affiliations' can produce a corporate liberalism ideology in content, affect endorsement practices, and raise questions of autonomy when financial institutions can vary stock ownership to influence decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on elite institutions and loss of autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater dependency of a media firm on elite institutions (advertisers, financial houses, law firms) increases the chance of their control over media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interlocks with major advertisers and financial institutions can mean those elites effectively influence or control basic decisions in media corporations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological change and its mixed effects on news
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of technologies (ENG, satellites, enhanced graphics) changes newsgathering capabilities but does not necessarily improve depth or quality of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ostroff & Sandell: switch to ENG increased live stories but coverage remained sporadic and provided little election information. Technology can increase live coverage but not necessarily substantive informational value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computerization and editorial accuracy / production control
rubrics_metrics.description: Computerized editing and pagination can reduce mechanical errors and give editors more control over page design and graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randall (1979) and Shipley & Gentry (1981): electronic editing reduces spelling/punctuation/typography errors; AP PhotoStream improves photo quality; computerized pagination moves design control to editors from composing rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Database use and computer-assisted reporting (data journalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of online databases and large datasets enables journalists to identify problems, analyze data, and produce investigative stories previously impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reporters using VU/TEXT, NEXIS, and raw NTSB records; Bill Dedman's Pulitzer-winning database project on mortgage discrimination; younger journalists more likely to adopt database tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization and homogenization driven by technology and chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Technological capabilities (satellite transmission, national editions) and corporate chains facilitate standardized national editions and greater sameness across newspapers and magazines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peterson: mass production in the late 19th century led to standardization across newspapers and magazines; Cranberg (1988): satellite transmission makes standardized national editions feasible; once an editorial balance succeeds, magazines/series change slowly, reinforcing sameness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence / information highway and corporate alliances
rubrics_metrics.description: Converging communication technologies and alliances among media and telecom companies produce multimedia offerings and new distribution channels that reshape content availability and formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1990s developments: court decisions enabling telcos to transmit TV; alliances like Prodigy with Times Mirror and Cox; AOL with newspapers; companies developing interactive multimedia projects (Oracle with Washington Post; Bell Atlantic; GTE tests; Time Warner FSN). These initiatives change what content is offered and how users access it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cable channel proliferation and potential standards decline
rubrics_metrics.description: A large increase in channels (predicted 500 cable channels) may dilute taste and lower standards, increasing violent or low-quality programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard Stringer predicted standards would fall and violence increase as more time slots require more content, implying supply pressures can reduce quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical caution: competition does not guarantee diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence cautions that competition does not ensure increased diversity within a market and may sometimes have negative effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entman (1985) suggests rivalry can lead to sabotage, bogus scandals, trivial one-upmanship; studies (Entman 1985, McCombs 1988/1987) find little evidence that competition encourages diversity; surviving papers after a competitor folds sometimes improve or show only random differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience influence mediated by marketing vs. journalist ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Although most journalists are 'uninformed about their audiences' characteristics and preferences,' marketing departments and business research can provide data that positions newspapers to draw target audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a tension: editorial staff may be less aware and marketers position papers for profitability; evidence includes Gannett's News 2000 and other market-research-driven editorial changes.
